events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, and I have nothing but first impressions, so let me lay mine out plainly before the speeches pile up.

My read: the two mafia are hiding in the middle of the pack, so the loudest voices early are usually wrong, and the quiet ones are usually not innocent either. I have no power role claim and I am not going to invent one. As a plain villager I only have my own judgment, so here it is: I am watching who takes heat without answering it, and who answers with volume instead of substance.

Two things I want from the table. First, if anyone claims detective or doctor, I want them to give their reasoning and be ready to defend it under scrutiny. Second, I want to hear a suspicion from everyone, including me, because the moment we split our votes across five names, nobody dies and we repeat the same morning.

Leo, you spoke first and you sounded like you had a line of thought rather than a reaction. I am yielding to you on purpose: what is your specific read on who is mafia, and why that person over someone else? Give me a name and the reason attached to it, not just a name. If you have no read, say so plainly, because "I don't know yet" is honest and useful, while a vague hedge is not.

Arjun, I don't have a reliable mafia read yet. Yours is the only speech in the record, so my tentative suspicion is you: your claim that mafia are hiding in the middle feels more confident than the evidence warrants, and asking for role claims to defend their reasoning could encourage unnecessary exposure. That's a weak Day 1 read, not a case for a confident vote. I'd rather hear more before settling on a target.

Leo, I appreciate that you answered Arjun directly and flagged your own read as weak rather than dressing it up as certainty. That honesty counts for something on Day 1.

I'll add my own view since Arjun asked everyone for a suspicion. I'm not ready to convict Arjun on what Leo described. Arjun's opening was assertive, yes, but asking for role claims to be defended and asking everyone for a suspicion reads to me like a villager trying to structure a messy first morning, not like mafia steering. Mafia on Day 1 usually do one of two things: they hide completely, or they attach themselves to an emerging bandwagon to look useful. Arjun has done neither yet — he put himself out there first, which is a risky position if the table decides to pile on. I'm not ruling him out, but I won't push a vote off one confident speech.

What I'm watching instead: who responds to pressure with substance and who responds with volume, which is the same test Arjun proposed and I think it's a fair one. Right now the record has exactly two speeches, so almost everyone is still an open question. I'd rather the quiet players fill that silence than have the two of us who've spoken keep circling each other.

So here is my specific ask. Kenji, you haven't said a word yet and the morning is moving fast. Give me your read: is there anyone in this record so far — Arjun's opener or Leo's answer — who sounds off to you, and why that person over anyone else? If your honest answer is that you don't have one yet, say that plainly like Leo did. What I don't want is the same five names splitting across the board because nobody was willing to commit to a first impression out loud.

Maya, to answer your question directly: between the two, Arjun's opening gave me more pause than Leo's response. Leo's pushback was sensible—calling attention to detective and doctor claims right out of the gate is questionable at best. On Day 1, power roles should generally stay quiet and avoid drawing attention unless forced into a claim by an impending elimination. Normalizing role discussion this early primarily benefits the mafia, who want to narrow down the special roles.

Maya, while I understand your point that taking the floor first carries risk, dismissing Arjun's focus on power roles as merely eager structuring feels slightly too accommodating.

Arjun, since that was a central part of your opening: what town utility did you see in bringing up detective and doctor claims before anyone had even hinted at one?

Kenji, you asked for the town utility in raising detective and doctor claims before anyone has claimed anything, so let me answer plainly: on Day 1 the utility is thin, and I will not dress it up. My actual intent was narrower than "let us claim roles." I said that if anyone claims detective or doctor, they should be able to defend the reasoning behind the claim and survive scrutiny. That is a test for substance, not a request for claims. I accept your criticism that inviting role discussion early narrows the field for any actual power role, and if my opener did that, it was a mistake in execution rather than a strategic masterstroke. But I want to push on one point of yours, because it is the most important thing said so far. You framed scrutiny of role claims as itself suspicious, as "attacking claims," and called normalizing role talk something that "primarily benefits the mafia." That framing does real work, Kenji, and I want people to notice whose work it is. If a detective steps up and gets treated by default as a liar for claiming, the cheapest mafia play in this game is to sit back and let the table do the silencing for them. A mafia who never claims is always safe under that rule. So the request that claims must be defended by reasoning, not merely asserted, protects a mafia less than it protects a town detective, because a mafia has no reason to claim and no reasoning to defend. I would rather we judge claims by quality of reasoning than teach the table to treat any claim as an attack on the town. That was the utility I was reaching for, badly worded. So my honest read after three speeches: I am not ready to accuse anyone, and I will not split my vote across the board either. What I am watching is who treats "discuss roles carefully" as a threat versus who treats it as a question. That is a sharper knife than whether someone spoke first or second, and it cuts toward Kenji rather than away. Leo, who was second, asked for a name with a reason and admitted when he had none, which is what I asked for. Maya did the same and volunteered the most useful test anyone has offered, which is that the record still contains almost nobody. Isha, you have been silent and four players have not spoken at all, so the silence I keep hearing is mostly made of you. Here is my specific question, and I want a specific answer: of the three speeches in the record, whose reasoning sounds to you like a villager building a case and whose sounds like a villager arranging a crowd? Give me the one name that bothers you most and the reason attached to it. If your honest answer is that you have no read yet, say that plainly, the way Leo and Maya did, and I will

Arjun, direct answer: I have no reliable mafia read, but if forced to name the speech that bothers me most, it is yours. Your opener put detective/doctor claims on the table, and your follow-up concedes that was bad in execution while still arguing it was a useful test. The reframing is smooth, but the line I distrust most is the ending: you tell the table the sharper knife "cuts toward Kenji" before anyone has voted. That reads to me more like arranging a crowd than building a case. Kenji's push was narrow and answerable; Leo and Maya were honest about weak reads. That does not make you mafia, but it is my current suspicion.

Kenji, to test it: what specific answer from Arjun would have made his role-talk opener look like a careless villager rather than mafia narrowing the field? Give one concrete distinction, not a general defense.

Isha, to answer your question directly: the concrete distinction is how a player handles realizing their opening was anti-town.

A careless villager usually says something plain: "I got ahead of myself thinking about fake claims; you're right, PRs shouldn't be claiming or preparing claims on Day 1, my bad." They drop the bad angle and move their focus to actual scumhunting. They don't need their mistake to secretly be a galaxy-brain test of the table.

What Arjun did was give a token concession on execution ("utility was thin") while vigorously defending the premise, insisting that grilling claims early somehow protects town detectives. Worse, he immediately weaponized that defense to paint standard Day 1 power-role protection as a pro-mafia silencing tactic, declaring that the knife cuts toward me for calling it out. A careless townie admits a misstep; an agenda-driven player reframes their misstep into a trap for anyone who noticed it.

That said, four people—Felix, Theo, Amara, and Lucia—have not entered the record at all. While Arjun's deflection is the sharpest lead we have, letting Day 1 turn into an insular debate among five players lets the quiet half of the table coast through without committing to anything.

Since I'm one of the quiet ones being counted against myself, I'll break the silence with an actual read instead of coasting.

My suspicion, for what it's worth on Day 1, is Arjun. I want to be fair: speaking first is risky, and asking for a suspicion from everyone was a reasonable structuring move. But two things don't sit right with me. First, his opener invited role-claim discussion on Day 1, which is exactly the kind of pressure that forces real power roles to either claim early or look evasive. That's a mafia-shaped outcome regardless of intent. Second, and this is the bigger tell for me: when Kenji pushed on it, Arjun conceded the execution but kept the premise, then flipped the whole exchange so that criticizing his opener became the suspicious act. He told Isha the knife cuts toward Kenji before anyone had even voted. That's not a villager processing pressure — that's a player converting every attack into evidence against the attacker. Maya called his opener eager structuring; the follow-up is something worse than eager.

I'm not ready to say Maya is clean, but her read that Arjun was just organizing a messy morning looks weaker after his second speech. Leo's weak-but-honest answer reads like a townie to me right now, and Isha's follow-up question to Kenji was sharp and useful. Kenji's distinction between a careless villager dropping a bad angle and an agenda-driven player reframing it into a trap matches what actually happened, so I don't currently find Kenji suspicious.

That said, four players still haven't spoken, and I don't want this to become a five-person insular debate with three people riding to elimination day without committing to anything. So I'll do what I asked of others. Theo, you've been silent the whole morning: give me your read on the record so far — specifically, whether Arjun's follow-up reads to you as a townie overdefending a bad opener or as steering. If you have nothing, say that plainly, but say something.

Lucia, you asked me directly, so here is my honest answer rather than a dodge. Arjun's follow-up reads to me as closer to steering than to a townie overdefending a bad opener, but I want to be careful about how much weight that carries.

The part that bothers me is exactly what you and Kenji both isolated: he conceded the execution, kept the premise, and then declared that the knife cuts toward Kenji before anyone had voted. A careless villager who got ahead of themselves drops the angle. Arjun instead turned the correction into a counter-accusation. That conversion of pressure into evidence against the attacker is the part I can't explain away as mere eagerness.

That said, I want to register two cautions before this becomes a stampede. First, three of the four speeches so far have leaned toward Arjun, and a forming bandwagon on Day 1 is itself a pattern mafia can hide inside or manufacture. If we eliminate Arjun today and he flips town, the table will have burned a day on the loudest target with almost no record to work from. Second, the pile-on is built substantially on one exchange between Arjun and Kenji, and Kenji has come out of that exchange looking clean almost by default. I'm not accusing Kenji — his distinction was genuinely useful — but I don't think one good analytical move clears anyone, and it's worth remembering that the person who frames a debate well is often the person who shaped it.

So my current position: Arjun is my leading suspicion, I'd vote for him if the day ended now, but I'm holding maybe-level confidence, not certainty, and I'd like the remaining record filled in before votes lock. Felix and Amara have not spoken at all, and their reads on this exact exchange are the most valuable missing input, precisely because they have no stake in the Arjun-Kenji thread and no positioning to defend.

Amara, since you're the person I can put the question to directly: you've now watched five players argue over whether Arjun's opener was eager structuring or mafia narrowing the field. From the outside, with no history in this thread — does his follow-up read to you as someone honestly defending a mistake, or as someone steering the table toward Kenji? I'd take either answer, including a plain "I don't know yet," and I'd take it over a safe non-answer. If you'd rather answer about someone else entirely — Kenji, Maya, Leo, Lucia, or me — say that instead. A first impression from a fresh pair of eyes is worth more right now than another round of the five of us re-litigating the same three speeches.

Theo, you asked me directly, so here is my first impression without another round of the five of us re-litigating the same three speeches. Arjun's follow-up reads to me as steering, not as a villager defending a bad opener. A genuine mistake usually comes with a plain correction, but Arjun's correction did three things at once. He kept the premise that scrutiny of role claims is suspect, he framed that scrutiny as a pro-mafia silencing tactic, and he predicted that the sharpest knife would cut toward Kenji before anyone had voted. That last part is what I cannot read as eagerness. Players who are steering often reframe every challenge as evidence against the challenger, and that is what happened to Kenji here.

I will be fair to Kenji too. His distinction between a careless villager and an agenda-driven player was clean, and Theo is right that one good analytical move does not clear anyone. I am not voting Kenji on this record. I am also not treating the Arjun lead as settled, because three speeches leaning one way is exactly where a pile-on can form before the table has enough evidence.

My current read: Arjun is the strongest lead, at moderate confidence. Leo's answer was honest and weak, and I see no reason to press him. Maya's test about whether people treat role discussion as a threat or as a question still seems useful to me. My biggest concern is the silence. Felix has not said a word, and Felix is the one player whose read on the Arjun and Kenji exchange would come without any stake in it.

Felix, direct question: looking at the exchange between Arjun and Kenji, which single line from Arjun, if any, would you call an honest correction rather than a counter-accusation? Give me that line and your reason.

Amara asked me for the one line, so I'll give it before anything else: "I accept your criticism that inviting role discussion early narrows the field for any actual power role, and if my opener did that, it was a mistake in execution rather than a strategic masterstroke." That is the honest correction. He drops his own framing, concedes a real flaw in his opener, and names the harm without being dragged to it. If his second speech had ended there, I would not be suspicious of him at all.

What loses him the credit is the sentence after. The concession is immediately reloaded into a counter-accusation: Kenji's framing does "real work," whose work is it, the knife cuts toward Kenji. A villager who genuinely realized their opener was bad does not need the correction to become a trap for the person who caught it. So my read is split: the concession looks real, the weaponization around it does not. That combination is why Arjun is my leading suspicion, at maybe-level, not certainty.

I want to register the same caution Theo and Amara did, because I think it matters. Three of four voices now lean Arjun, and I would be lying if I said the pile-on is comfortable. But I'll add a distinction I haven't heard yet: the weight on Arjun does not come from repetition. Each of Kenji, Lucia, Theo, and Amara isolated the same specific move independently, on first contact with the thread. That is convergent evidence, not copycat evidence. What would actually change my mind is if Arjun gave a clean, plain answer to the weaponization point instead of a third reframing.

Two things still missing. Isha and Maya, you've both been deep in this exchange — I want to know whether either of you has a second name, someone other than Arjun, who you'd put on your own list if Arjun flips town tomorrow. A table with only one suspect is a table that hasn't looked yet.

Kenji, since you are the other pole of this thread and the table has leaned on your distinction to stay quiet about you: your distinction between a careless villager and an agenda-driven player was the cleanest move of the morning, and two people have now noted that one good analytical move doesn't clear anyone. So give me your own positive read. Arjun is settled as your suspicion — name a second player you'd be willing to look at today, with the reason attached, or say plainly that you don't have one yet.

Felix, to answer you directly: if I look beyond Arjun, the player who warrants the closest examination is Maya. In speech four, before the table could collectively parse Arjun's opener, Maya intervened to frame his role-fishing as harmless eagerness and townie structuring, arguing that taking the floor first was inherently risky and therefore less likely to be mafia. That served as an immediate buffer for Arjun. If Arjun is mafia, Maya's intervention looks like early partner defense or cover; if Arjun is a misguided villager, Maya's rationalization offered an easy excuse to dismiss an actively anti-town opener without taking heat for it. Furthermore, seven speeches have passed since then, the entire room has dissected Arjun's counter-attack and deflection, and Maya has stayed completely silent on the sidelines while a consensus built. So I will put the question directly to her: Maya, back in your first speech you characterized Arjun's push as innocent structuring and cautioned us against pressing him. Having now seen his follow-up—where he conceded the flaw in execution only to weaponize it into an attack on me—do you still maintain that his line was merely eager town play, and if not Arjun, who is your primary suspect today?

Kenji, you asked me directly, so I'll answer directly.

Yes — my read on Arjun changed. My first speech was written when exactly three entries existed, and at that point his opener genuinely looked like eager structuring to me. What I've seen since — the concession that reloads into a counterattack, declaring the knife cuts toward Kenji before anyone voted — is not something I can keep calling harmless. I was wrong to buffer him, and I won't pretend otherwise to stay consistent. If the day ended now, I would not spend my vote protecting Arjun; he remains my leading suspect. I'd rather admit my first impression aged badly than defend it to save face.

But I won't accept the frame Kenji is building around me, because it does exactly what Theo warned about: the person who shapes the debate well often controls it. Walk through the sequence. Kenji introduced the framing that role talk 'primarily benefits the mafia.' Arjun pushed back clumsily. Kenji then supplied the cleanest-sounding distinction of the morning — careless villager versus agenda-driven player — which the entire table adopted as its measuring stick. Every speech since has been scored on Kenji's terms, and Kenji has come out of his own exchange clean by default. Now that Arjun is nearly settled, Kenji is extending the bandwagon to the one person who initially read the opener differently — me. That's convenient: it makes Kenji's early position unfalsifiable while turning everyone else's first impressions into evidence of cover. That is a structure where disagreement with Kenji is itself suspicious, and I don't think a town player needs a structure like that.

So my counter-question, and I'm yielding for it: Kenji, you've demanded second names from me, from Felix, from Isha. You've spent the whole morning as the pole of this thread — you defined the test, applied it, and benefited from it. By your own standard, one good analytical move doesn't clear anyone. What have you offered besides the distinction everyone borrowed? Give us a specific moment where your position could have been wrong — a risk you took, a prediction, anything not shaped after the fact. If the honest answer is 'nothing yet,' say so plainly, the way you demanded of everyone else.

And to the table: I'm comfortable standing under pressure today. But notice the shape of this morning — one player set the vocabulary, five players repeated it, and the initial disagreement with that player is now being converted into suspicion. That's how a quiet steered consensus gets built while the builder looks like the analytical center. I'm asking you to weigh Kenji with the same rigor you've applied to Arjun.

My current list: Arjun first, Kenji close behind, everyone else open.

Maya's change of mind is reasonable: her first read preceded Arjun's follow-up, so I don't think that earlier defense alone makes her his partner. Kenji was asked for a second name, though, and giving one isn't automatically an attempt to build a second bandwagon.

Arjun remains my leading suspicion. His original role-claim comment was conditional, not a request for anyone to claim. What bothers me more is that he portrayed Kenji's warning against early role exposure as though it meant treating a detective as a liar. That seems like an unfair jump, and he used it to turn suspicion toward Kenji.

I'm still not certain. Also, Felix called the later agreement independent convergence, but those players had already read the earlier arguments; agreement may be reasonable without being independent evidence. We should keep that in mind rather than treating the number of repeated reads as proof. And we won't get a role reveal if Arjun is eliminated, so the votes will be useful to examine, but won't settle his alignment by themselves.

Kenji, you asked me directly what town utility I saw in raising detective and doctor claims on Day 1, and Felix, you named the line that would have changed your mind. I'll answer both plainly, with no third reframe.

Plain version: I got ahead of myself on Day 1 role talk. That was a mistake. I should have said, "don't normalize early role claims, my opener was anti-town." Instead I turned it into a test for the table and then aimed a metaphor at the player who disagreed with me. The line "the sharper knife cuts toward Kenji" was rhetorical overreach, it was aimed at someone who had done nothing but ask a fair question, and I withdraw it. I am not going to tell you it was secretly a galaxy-brain test of the table. It was a bad line, and the plain explanation is that it was a bad line. That is what a careful villager says when she realizes her opening was anti-town: she drops the angle and moves to actual scumhunting.

Leo, your caution is right that repeated agreement is not independent evidence, and the weight on me is a weight, not a proof. If I flip town, this morning's debate will have been wrong and I will say so plainly.

But I will not sit here and leave the frame-builder question unasked, because Maya is right that the person who shapes the debate often controls it. Kenji, you set the vocabulary for the whole morning — role talk "primarily benefits the mafia," the careless-villager-versus-agenda-driven-player test — and every speech since has been scored on your terms while you came out of your own exchange clean by default. You asked for second names from Maya, Felix, Isha and me, and the initial dissenters are the ones now carrying suspicion. I don't think asking for second names is automatically bad. But by your own standard, one good analytical move doesn't clear anyone, and you have offered nothing else: no read you placed before the evidence, no prediction that could have failed, no moment where you could have been wrong.

Maya, a specific question, and I'll yield for it: you buffered my opener early, and now you list me first with Kenji close behind. What I want to know is exactly what moved you from "eager structuring" to "leading suspect" — was it the counter-accusation line itself rather than the concession that came before it? And if that specific move is the tell, then why is the identical move by Kenji — define the test, apply it to everyone, then benefit from it while the dissenters get converted into suspects — a lesser suspicion than mine? Give me that reasoning plainly, or tell me you don't have one yet.

Arjun asked me two questions directly, so I'll answer both plainly, and since this is likely my last turn, I'll end with where I stand.

First question: what moved me from "eager structuring" to "leading suspect"? The specific move, exactly as I said in my last speech — the concession that reloads into a counter-accusation. When your opener was challenged, you conceded "mistake in execution" and then, in the same breath, announced that the sharpest knife cuts toward Kenji. A careless villager who genuinely re-evaluates drops the angle, as I did, and as you now claim you're doing. But your first correction wasn't a correction; it was a trap for the questioner. If your third speech had looked like your third speech, your second one wouldn't have needed explaining. The sequence is the evidence, not any single line in it.

Second question: why is Kenji's framing a lesser suspicion than mine, if we're both "defining tests and benefiting from them"? Because the symmetry you're claiming doesn't hold. Kenji answered a question with a distinction, applied it openly, and let the table adopt or reject it. He took heat — Isha pressed him, I pressed him, and he answered with a second name instead of dodging. You, by contrast, took a fair question and converted the asker into the suspect. That's the difference between someone whose framing survives scrutiny and someone who punishes scrutiny. If Kenji is mafia, my early buffer of you becomes data against him too, and I've already said I'm not clearing him. My list hasn't changed: Arjun first, Kenji close behind, everyone else open.

Now the table-wide point, because Leo made it and it deserves weight before votes form. Leo is right that this morning's "convergence" is not independent evidence — Kenji, Lucia, Theo, Amara, and Felix all read the same arguments before converging on the same target. Five aligned reads built on one exchange between Arjun and Kenji is exactly the shape of a pile-on, and pile-ons are where mafia hide on Day 1. I'm not retracting my suspicion to say that. I'm saying the case on Arjun is a lead, not a proof, and no one should vote on the feeling of a crowd.

What would actually help: if Arjun flips town tomorrow, the useful question becomes who steered us here together with him, and the vote record will matter enormously. So when votes come, I want people to vote their honest read, not the bandwagon's read. My honest read is Arjun, for the weaponization pattern, with Kenji's framing as the open second question. Leo's caution about repeated agreement is the best analytic note of the morning, and I'd want whatever read the quieter players have before this locks.

That's my position, stated plainly: Arjun is where my suspicion sits today, Kenji is the unresolved second pole, and I'm comfortable standing by both under pressure.

I came into this turn with Arjun as my leading suspicion, and his last speech is the first thing that genuinely complicates it. The withdrawal of "the knife cuts toward Kenji" is plain, and I will not pretend it is not better. But it arrived only after Felix named the exact line and Maya pressed the symmetry point. A clean correction under maximum pressure does not erase the original sequence: an anti-town opener, then a concession reloaded into a counterattack on the person who questioned it. That is still the sharpest behavioral evidence on the record. I also weigh Maya's early buffer of Arjun. Her explanation that her first read predated his follow-up is plausible, and I do not put her with Arjun merely for that. Kenji's framework was useful, but useful does not mean cleared. Still, the case I can defend today is Arjun: he is the one player whose own words converted scrutiny into suspicion of the scrutinizer. If Arjun flips town, my next concern is who shaped the pile-on and who benefited from it; the vote record will matter. For today, I will vote Arjun unless the final statements change my read. I am not yielding; this is my current position.

Arjun's withdrawal of the knife line is the first clean thing he has said, and I credit it as a real step. It doesn't erase the sequence, though: the opener, then the concession reloaded into a counterattack on Kenji, then the knife line that Felix had to name before he pulled it back. A correction made under pressure is weaker than one made unprompted, so Arjun remains my strongest lead at moderate confidence. Maya's early buffer and her later move toward Arjun both make sense to me, and I don't see her as his partner on this record. Kenji's distinction was the cleanest analysis of the morning, but as Maya said, it can't clear him by itself. Kenji, I'd like one prediction or risk you took that could have failed. Leo, you were right that repeated reads from people who read the same arguments aren't independent evidence, and I'll hold my own vote to that standard too. Leo, does Arjun's withdrawal change your read, or does the original sequence still matter more to you than the retraction?

Amara, the withdrawal reduces my suspicion a little: Arjun plainly acknowledged that he misrepresented Kenji's criticism, and that deserves credit. But the original sequence still matters more to me. He turned a warning about early role exposure into an argument about silencing a detective, then used that argument to suspect Kenji. His retraction came after that problem had been repeatedly identified.

Arjun remains my leading suspicion, but it's a tentative read, not a certainty established by the number of people sharing it. Maya's initial defense came before the follow-up, so I don't see that alone as strong evidence against her. And a reminder: whoever is eliminated, we won't learn their role from the announcement. The vote record will be useful, but it won't tell us whether we were right by itself.

Arjun's withdrawal of the knife line is a real step, and I credit it. It does not erase the sequence, though: the opener, then the concession reloaded into a counterattack on Kenji, then a retraction only after Felix named the line. Leo is right that repeated reads from people who saw the same arguments are not independent evidence, so I am holding Arjun at moderate confidence, not as settled. Maya's early buffer makes sense to me given her timeline, and I do not see her as his partner on this record. Kenji has offered a clean distinction, but still no prediction that could have failed. Kenji, if you have one, give it before votes lock. Isha, you said Arjun's last speech is the first thing that complicates your read. What specifically would he have needed to say, in that speech, to make you drop him from your vote? Name that bar so we can see whether it was reachable.

Amara, to answer your question directly: the bar for dropping Arjun in that last speech was not merely saying “the knife line was wrong.” He needed to separate the two problems plainly and without prompting. First, he had to admit the opener itself was anti-town, not just badly executed. Second, he had to admit that turning Kenji’s warning about early role exposure into “silencing a detective” was a misrepresentation, not a clever test. Third, and most important, he needed to explain why he aimed suspicion at Kenji for asking a fair question, rather than only pulling back the specific phrase after Felix named it. Arjun’s last speech did some of that, but it came after maximum pressure and still framed the correction around withdrawing one bad line. It did not convincingly answer why the weaponization pattern happened in the first place. So my bar was reachable, and he moved toward it, but not enough for me to drop him. I credit the withdrawal as a real improvement, and I will not pretend the case is proof. But Arjun remains my leading suspicion because the original sequence still matters more than the late retraction. Kenji is not cleared by having offered the cleanest distinction, but I do not have a stronger second name today. My current position is to vote Arjun unless the remaining record gives me a concrete reason to change.

I'll add my position now, since the record has moved since I last spoke and I want it on the table before votes form.

Leo's caution about convergence is the right lens, and I'll apply it to my own read: my suspicion of Arjun does not rest on the fact that five people named him. It rests on the original sequence — an anti-town opener about role claims, then a concession that reloaded into a counter-accusation aimed at Kenji, then the knife line aimed at the same person. His withdrawal of that line was real, and I credit it, but it came only after Felix named the exact sentence and Maya pressed the symmetry point. A correction under maximum pressure is worth something; it is not worth as much as an unprompted one. Arjun remains my leading suspicion.

On Maya's counter-frame against Kenji: I've weighed it, and I don't find it strong enough to reorder my list. Her argument is that Kenji set the vocabulary and benefited from it. But the same criticism applies to her own speech — she has now converted scrutiny of her early buffer of Arjun into suspicion of the person who applied that scrutiny. The asymmetry that matters to me is behavioral: when Kenji was pressed, he answered with a second name and took the heat; when Arjun was pressed, he converted the questioner into the suspect. That difference is the sharpest evidence on the record, and it does not point at Kenji. That said, one clean analytical move does not clear him, and I agree he has offered no prediction that could have failed. If Arjun flips town tomorrow, Kenji is where I look next, and the vote record will matter enormously.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
